title: Book X
frozenSupport: Book X opens by questioning whether the soul will ever become good, simple, one, naked, affectionate, and content with what the gods assign.
Marcus grounds this in part-whole reasoning: the part should not resent what benefits the whole, and the rational animal is also social.
The chapter includes a maintained-identity sequence around being good, modest, true, rational, equanimous, and magnanimous without caring to be called such.
It repeatedly attacks distraction, vanity, fear, and complaint by contemplating change, mortality, insignificance, and the sameness of places and people.
Late in the chapter Marcus sharpens self-audit with commands to stop talking about the good man and to ask what the ruling faculty is now making itself.
allowedClaims: simplicity in Book X means stripped, rational sufficiency rather than passivity
contentment is tied to belonging to the whole and to social nature
Marcus uses moral names as disciplines to inhabit, not labels to seek
change contemplation is meant to reduce vanity and complaint
the ruling faculty remains the decisive site of self-government
doNotClaim: that Book X teaches emotional numbness
that contentment means liking every circumstance
that social duty disappears once the soul is inwardly simplified
that simplicity is merely aesthetic minimalism
